beats.label: goosebumps
lines: Your skin can react to a memory, even when nothing touches you.
Goosebumps start with your sympathetic nervous system, which handles fight-or-flight.
Cold makes tiny arrector pili muscles contract and pull hairs upright.

beats.title: Feeling versus physiology
lines: Here's the twist: strong emotions can trigger goosebumps, but why is less understood.
People report chills, but those feelings do not always match measured goosebumps.

beats.title: Raised hair across species
lines: In hairy mammals, raised hairs trap air for insulation.
Some animals look bigger to intimidate enemies.
Porcupines raise quills when threatened; sea otters raise hair when meeting sharks.
For humans, some scientists call stress-related goosebumps a vestigial reflex.
Next time a powerful memory moves you, check your skin for bumps.
Your feeling of chills and your visible goosebumps may not match.

sources.claim: Goosebumps occur when arrector pili muscles contract and pull hairs upright, and the reflex begins in the sympathetic nervous system.
Strong and remembered emotions can cause goosebumps, but emotional correlates are not well understood, and self-reported goosebumps do not always match physiological piloerection.
Raised hairs trap air for insulation and can make animals appear larger; porcupines raise their quills when threatened, and sea otters raise hair when encountering sharks.
The formation of goosebumps in humans under stress is considered by some to be a vestigial reflex.

youtube.title: Why Do We Get Goosebumps? The Ancient Reflex Inside
youtube.description: Cold, emotion, and memory can trigger piloerection. Here's the muscle reflex behind your goosebumps—and why other animals use theirs.
